certainty_reasoning: Cook states flatly that 'Ives slept with Lord Alfred Douglas at the Albany' and, quoting the Ives diary in the source, records the night Ives refused a third man ('thought it wouldn't do in the Albany') and Ives's own words 'I had no objection to the thing itself'. Corroboration: Cook returns to this in Queer Domesticities (2014) p. 99, where the sexual relationship is stated in his own voice as settled background - the anecdote turns on his refusing a *third* man, not on the fact of the pair.
date_label: Oct. 1893 (introduced at Wilde's Savoy dinner, 15 Oct.) - mid-1890s; the Albany night(s) undated by Cook, necessarily after 30 June 1894 (E4 move-in). Attachment ended when 'Douglas turned on Wilde' (Ives marked him 'traitor' in the diary; undated).
summary: A brief liaison within the Wilde circle: Wilde brought Ives and Douglas together at a Savoy dinner on 15 October 1893 (recorded in Ives's diary), and Douglas visited and spent at least one night at Ives's chambers at E4 the Albany, where Ives refused to allow a third man to join them - 'it wouldn't do in the Albany'. Ives's diary records that he repeatedly warned Douglas over his recklessness while having 'no objection to the thing itself', and after Douglas turned on Wilde, Ives wrote 'traitor' against his name.

sources.quote: I warned Lord A more than once that he was indulging in homosexuality to a reckless and highly dangerous degree. For tho' I had no objection to the thing itself we were all afraid he would get arrested any day.
sources.context: Ives diary (undated entry), quoted by Cook; the sentence runs across Cook's page turn
sources.supports: Promoted to lead by the Q2 quality pass : the only passage on this edge in which a participant speaks, and the most explicit characterization available of what Ives thought he was doing with Douglas. The clause that carries it is 'I had no objection to the thing itself' - Ives conceding the sex and objecting only to the risk of arrest, which is as close to a plain statement of a sexual relationship as either man left. Ives's diary, undated entry, as quoted by Cook (2003); Cook prints no more of it than this, so the fuller text remains a target in the Ives papers and in Kaplan (2005).
sources.provenance: PDF pages 162-163, printed folios 146-147 confirmed on rendered pages.
sources.speaker: George Ives, diary

sources.quote: Ives slept with Lord Alfred Douglas at the Albany, and he also enjoyed uninterrupted meals there, at his former chambers in St James', and at nearby clubs with Wilde, Edward Carpenter, Robert Ross, Oscar Browning and others.
sources.context: Cook, on bachelor chambers as a screen for 'the sexual and social lives of wealthy men in London'
sources.supports: Ives slept with Douglas at the Albany (Cook's assertion, resting on the Ives diary)
sources.provenance: PDF page 48, printed folio 32 confirmed on rendered page.

sources.quote: It was also here that he spent the night with Lord Alfred Douglas, though he refused to allow a third party to join them because he 'thought it wouldn't do in the Albany'. The episode reveals Ives' enduring sense of propriety and reservation.
sources.context: Cook, on Ives's household at E4 the Albany (occupied from 30 June 1894); the inner quote is Cook quoting the Ives diary
sources.supports: Douglas spent the night at Ives's Albany rooms; Ives refused a third man, in the diary's words 'thought it wouldn't do in the Albany'
sources.provenance: PDF page 162, printed folio 146 confirmed on rendered page.

sources.quote: Ives had moved into E4 Albany in Piccadilly on 30 June. According to his diary 'O[scar] and B[osie] came to tea' on 5 July.
sources.context: Holland & Hart-Davis, editorial note to Wilde's letter to Ives of [circa 30 June 1894]
sources.supports: Douglas at Ives's Albany rooms, 5 July 1894 (diary); fixes the E4 move-in at 30 June 1894, so the Albany night(s) postdate it
sources.provenance: PDF page 644, printed folio 592 confirmed on rendered page.

sources.quote: He refused to allow a third man to join him and Lord Alfred Douglas, Wilde's intimate friend, for sex, for example, because 'it wouldn't do at the Albany'.
sources.context: Cook on Ives's discretion at the Albany
sources.supports: Cook states in his own voice that Ives and Douglas had sex at the Albany - the refusal is of a third participant only, and the stated reason is decorum rather than disinclination.
sources.provenance: PDF p. 110 (printed folio 99 confirmed on the rendered page).

sources.quote: This concern evaporated when Douglas turned on Wilde: Ives added the words 'traitor' to any mention of him in the diary.
sources.context: Cook, in the sentence immediately following Ives's 'no objection to the thing itself' passage; 'traitor' is Cook quoting Ives's own annotation
sources.supports: How Ives ended it, in Ives's own word. This record's summary already asserted the 'traitor' annotation without a source entry behind it; this supplies one. Note what the word is answering: Ives broke with Douglas over Douglas's conduct towards Wilde, not over anything between Douglas and himself. Ives's diary, undated, as quoted by Cook.
sources.provenance: PDF page 163 (printed folio 147 confirmed on the rendered page).

null_findings.finding: Kaplan, Sodom on the Thames, does not mention George Ives at any point - a whole-file search on the word boundary \bIves\b returns zero pages. The pointer that named Kaplan for the Albany nights and the refusal of the third man was mistaken and has been removed. Kaplan's 'Albany' references are to Albany Courtyard off Piccadilly in the Cleveland Street testimony.
